newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Heineken to expand Dutch brewing capacity.
newsitem.headline: Heineken to expand Dutch brewing capacity.

text.p: Heineken Netherlands, a unit of Heineken Breweries BV, will increase its capacity in the Netherlands by around 23 percent in the next three years to meet rising export demand, the company said on Monday.

Heineken will increase the capacity of its breweries in Den Bosch and Zoeterwoude, near Leiden, from 13 million hectolitres in 1995 to 16 million hectolitres in 1999, Rob Strobos, managing director of Heineken Netherlands, told a news conference.

The expansion was made necessary by continuing export growth, said Frans van der Minne, director for exports of parent Heineken Breweries. In 1996, exports reached 7 million hectolitres with export growth still around the 10 percent level, he said.
Exports to the U.S. accounted for 55 percent of that total, he added, but that revealed a rise to 45 percent in the share exported to other countries.
"That is in our opinion healthier than the situation ten years ago when the other countries formed a smaller part of the total," Van der Minne said.
Heineken Netherlands had formed a stategic partnership with Dutch firm Heye Glass in order to meet its increased demand for export bottles, Strobos said.
"We expect that our participation will bear fruit in terms of both quality and cost of our export bottles," he said.
But he added the step should not be taken to mean Heineken was diverging from its core activity as a brewer.

Total capacity at Heineken Netherland's brewery in Den Bosch would rise to 5.5 million hectolitres by 1999 from 4.5 million in 1995 and capacity in Zoeterwoude would grow to 10.5 million from 7.5 million, Production Director Han de Goederen said.

A new bottling line with a capacity of 90,000 bottles per hour was under construction in Den Bosch, while in Zoeterwoude a further 80,000 bottles an hour of packing capacity would come on line by October, he said.
"The process of re-engineering is going forward. We expect to have realised the predicted total capacity of 16 million hectolitres by 1999," De Goederen said.
